1.pericope_label: The Lord reigneth, let the people tremble: he that sitteth between the cherubim, and the first Holy is he

schools.summary: Augustine takes the reading that makes the peoples angry and refers it to the idolaters enraged when Christ began to be preached, and states as his whole design the finding of Christ in psalm, prophet and law alike.

Calvin holds the verb to cover any strong emotion of anger or fear and would read the clauses as futures, making the verse a prediction of the subjection of the nations; Gill reads the greatness in Zion of both temple and church.

Henry widens the trembling to the subjects and contrasts a former rule by holy fear with a present rule by holy love; Spurgeon asks a solemn yet joyful awe of the chosen and keeps both grandeur and nearness in the throne between the cherubim.

Clarke restricts the trembling to the opponents of the kingdom, reads the seat between the cherubim as a token of graciousness that survived the loss of the symbol, reviews the titles given by the versions, and hears the refrain as a solemn chorus; Wesley keeps to the enemies and to the presence of God with his people.

Ellicott reports the ancient rendering be angry and restores the ordinary present, prefers Holy is He as the refrain on grammatical grounds, and notes the rabbinic reading of the great and terrible name; Keil and Delitzsch make the threefold refrain the architecture of the psalm and argue from its exact measure for the integrity of the text.

debates: Do the peoples tremble or rage, and is the clause a wish or a statement? Ellicott reports that the old versions give be angry and that the optative of our version follows them, while the Hebrew is an ordinary present; Calvin holds the word to cover anger and fear alike and would read futures, making the verse a prediction; Augustine takes the anger and finds it in idolaters enraged by the preaching of Christ; and where Wesley and Clarke confine the trembling to enemies, Henry and Spurgeon extend it to the worshippers themselves.

How should the refrain be read and placed? Ellicott would render Holy is He rather than for it is holy, since the later occurrences require the masculine, and joins the following verse closely to this one; Clarke hears a chorus sung solemnly at the close of each part; Keil and Delitzsch make the refrain the architecture of the whole, dividing the psalm into three parts of two six-line stanzas each and arguing from that exactness against emendation.
outliers: Augustine states his method at the head of the psalm: since psalm, prophet and law were all written before the incarnation, the whole design in hearing them is to see Christ there and to understand Christ there.

Keil and Delitzsch support the measure of the psalm by an analogy from the creation week, in which the third and the sixth days each consist of two works, as each part here consists of two six-line stanzas.
themes: the reign of God as ground of worship
trembling as terror and as awe

4.pericope_label: The king strength loveth judgment: equity established, and worship at his footstool

schools.summary: Spurgeon makes the establishment of equity an institution as stable as the throne, insists that not even mercy will bend it, and complains that men of his day arraign the government of God where older saints submitted.
Gill reads the opening clause as it stands, of a mighty king who is no tyrant, and turns the call to exalt into a list of ways of doing it in heart, speech, private and public.

Clarke reads the verse of the human king as deputy whose strength and pattern were God himself, identifies the footstool with the ark, and keeps the refrain as a chorus burden; Wesley resolves the hard clause by a Hebraism and refers the refrain to the consecrated footstool rather than to God.

Keil and Delitzsch reject three constructions of the opening clause, including the division of the old Greek, and make the might the fronted object of the verb of establishing; Ellicott renders the command as prostration and locates the footstool at the ark or the ground beneath it.

debates: How is the clause about the king strength to be construed? Keil and Delitzsch reject the majority reading that carries it back over the refrain, deny that loving can be said of a strength rather than its possessor, set aside the old Greek division, and make the might the fronted object of the verb thou hast established; Wesley resolves the same difficulty by treating the king strength as a Hebraism for the powerful king; Gill and Spurgeon simply read a might that delights in right.

What is the footstool? Clarke lists the earth, the city, the temple, the tabernacle and the ark as things elsewhere so called and settles on the ark; Ellicott, since the throne above the cherubim has just been named, chooses either the ark or the ground on which it stood; Wesley takes it as the place before the ark.
outliers: Wesley refers the refrain of holiness to the footstool rather than to God, taking it to mean that the place is consecrated as a pledge of the divine presence.

Spurgeon distinguishes a court of equity from equity itself, observes that most kingdoms have an establishment and it is generally inequitable, and holds that here the executive is as righteous as the legislative.
themes: judgment executed and not only decreed

6.pericope_label: Moses and Aaron among his priests: the intercessors, the cloudy pillar, and the third Holy is he

schools.summary: Henry reports the Jewish title given to Moses as priest of the priests; Spurgeon makes him a true priest outside the typical order, as Melchizedek had been, distinguishes what each of the three saw of the divine holiness, and makes all three stand in the gap as intercessors.

Gill explains how Moses acted as priest before Aaron and consecrated him, notes that the speaking from the pillar ceased at the entry into the land, and asks whether Samuel too may have been answered out of a cloud.

Clarke reads the pillar as the means of directing every march and encampment and turns the keeping of the testimonies into an exhortation, and takes the vengeance as chastisement without consumption; Wesley separates the intercessors who were answered from the people who were forgiven.

Ellicott reads the three names as present rather than past, the ministers of the poet own day likened to the ancient heroes, and refers the vengeance to the community of his time as an unstated comparison; Keil and Delitzsch report and refute the reading that makes the three heavenly intercessors, and keep the plain historical sense.

debates: Do the three names belong to the past or the present? Ellicott renders a Moses and an Aaron and a Samuel, taking the poet to liken the ministers of his own day to the heroes of old, and argues that a historical reference would be inaccurate since Moses was no priest and Samuel was not addressed from the pillar; Keil and Delitzsch admit the present sound of the phrase but keep the historical sense, and every other voice reads plain narrative.

In what sense was Moses among the priests? Gill says he officiated before Aaron was called and himself consecrated him, Henry reports the Jewish title priest of the priests, Clarke and Wesley note that he held the office before the priesthood was instituted, Spurgeon makes him a true priest outside the typical order as Melchizedek was, and Ellicott turns the same difficulty into an argument that the passage is not historical at all.
outliers: Ellicott illustrates his reading with a modern analogy, that the poet speaks as we might in saying that we have a Newton or a Bacon among us.

Keil and Delitzsch report an expositor who took the three as heavenly intercessors after the manner of a vision in the later Jewish books, and refuse it because it presupposes an active life in those fallen asleep, contrary to what the psalms suppose about the other world.
themes: a priesthood outside the legal order
forgiveness that did not avert chastisement
